beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on grade mode: how the physics engine checks a student's own work. Here's the difference. A student submits minus one point nine six. A normal checker says, wrong. Grade mode says: your number matches what you get by reversing a difference. Check your sign convention.

props.command: A student answered a = −1.96 for the Atwood problem. What does the physics engine's grade mode tell them?
output: It names the mistake: a sign flip
It quotes the card's own warning
It never grades against an unverified answer

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, how grade mode names which mistake a student made. Second, how it finds the first step that went wrong. And third, the two things it refuses to do. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. Grade mode doesn't just mark answers. It diagnoses them. It compares the student's number with the verified answer, and with a set of specific wrong formulas: the classic mistakes. If the number matches one of those, the feedback names the mistake, and quotes the card's own warning.

beats.new_visual_element: wrong formulas, built from the right one
beats.narration_text: The list of mistakes is built from the correct formula itself. Flip the sign of a difference. Invert the whole thing. Lose, or gain, a factor of two. Be off by exactly the square root of two: the classic mix-up between escape speed and orbital speed. Or forget to take a square root. Each wrong version is computed, and compared with what the student wrote.

Back to the pulley. Masses of four and six kilograms. The right acceleration is one point nine six meters per second squared. A student writes minus one point nine six. That matches a sign flip exactly. So grade mode says so, and quotes the pulley card's warning: inconsistent sign convention across the two masses' equations. That's not just a grade. It's a lesson.

If the student shows their steps, grade mode finds the first one that went wrong. A spinning disk. The student's moment of inertia is zero point one two five. The reference is zero point zero six two five: exactly half. Grade mode points at the moment of inertia, not at the final spin speed. Everything after the first error is downstream of it.

It's also deliberately fair. Answers within two percent count as right, because students round. In the team's words, marking three point two wrong when the answer is three point two zero two six teaches nothing, except that the grader is pedantic. Every submission gets one of five results: correct, wrong value, wrong method, incomplete, or not assessable.

And two things it refuses to do. It won't grade against an answer it can't verify. That returns not assessable, and goes to a human. And it doesn't store anything. Grading needs a student's identity, so it takes the work, returns an assessment, and forgets. Saving graded work is a separate decision, still waiting on a privacy review. To be clear, nothing is deployed yet. No student has used it.

So here's the takeaway. Wrong is a verdict. Which mistake is feedback. When an A.I. model checks your work, don't settle for right or wrong. Ask which step went wrong first, and what mistake produces exactly your number.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with your own worked solution. It asks Claude to grade it the way grade mode does.

props.command: Here is a problem and my worked solution: [paste both]. Don't just say right or wrong. Tell me which, and why.
